header:
Date: 2027-09-10
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 60 minutes
Attendees: Sofia Chen (Redwood AE), Marcus Patel (Redwood SE), Diego Alvarez (Redwood SE), Jamal Rivers (Aurelius Head of ML Infra), Priya Das (Aurelius SRE), Lena Ortiz (Aurelius Security), Tom Becker (Aurelius Networking)
topics: Runtime performance: latency, throughput, tail latencies
Security: KMS, audit logs, VPC isolation
summary: Deep technical discussion focused on running Redwood Private in Aurelius' VPC. Main concerns: network topology (PrivateLink vs. VPN), NAT and egress, DNS resolution for internal endpoints, cross-AZ traffic, and how runtime features (KV cache, batching, quantization) interact with network latency. Agreed to run a 3-node benchmark and to share PrivateLink architecture + templates.
transcript:
[00:00] Sofia Chen: hey everyone, thanks for joining, we'll do a deep dive on private vpc networking and some runtime perf details, we've got about an hour
[00:12] Jamal Rivers: sounds good, want to make sure we cover the latency parts first, our customers are sensitive to 95th percentile token latency
[00:20] Marcus Patel: yeah totally, we'll walk through kv-cache behavior, batching, and then how network hops (privatelink, nat) affect tail latencies
[00:31] Priya Das: quick ask, we've got strict egress controls, we prefer privatelink over internet egress, does redwood support AWS privatelink or equivalents?
[00:44] Sofia Chen: yes, we support PrivateLink for the control plane and for RPCs to the runtime; there's a small control channel over PrivateLink and then data path options - either PrivateLink-backed endpoints or a VPC peering/ENI model depending on latency needs
[00:58] Tom Becker: can you explain the difference in hops? like when would a request traverse NAT vs privatelink?
[01:10] Diego Alvarez: sure, so with PrivateLink the client talks to an interface endpoint in your VPC that forwards directly to our service via the AWS network, that avoids internet NAT egress. If you choose dedicated on-prem or a self-hosted runtime you might use VPC peering or direct ENIs which have different cross-AZ considerations
[01:28] Jamal Rivers: ok and what about DNS? we have split-horizon DNS and internal resolvers, will the privatelink endpoints register there or do we have to create private hosted zones?
[01:40] Marcus Patel: typically you create a private hosted zone or use conditional forwarding to resolve the service domain to the interface endpoint. We'll provide example templates; the common pitfall is forgetting the VPC resolver rules which causes failover to public records
[01:56] Priya Das: noted. on the runtime side, how sensitive is the kv cache to a 1-2 ms network increase? some of our pods are cross AZ and we get variable latency
[02:10] Marcus Patel: good question. The KV cache is local to the runtime node (in-memory) for most scenarios. The main network sensitivity is if you're using a shared KV store across nodes or have remote parameter services. For our standard setup with local kv + sharded model state the network adds to RPCs for cold cache misses and model load, so a 1-2 ms increase might show up in the 95th pct on cold-starts but warm generation token-by-token latency is mostly compute-bound
[02:36] Jamal Rivers: so warm steady-state token latencies aren't super impacted by privatelink?
[02:42] Marcus Patel: correct, warm token generation is dominated by GPU/kernel time and KV cache hits. Network matters for batching coordination and large context fetches (like when we pull KV for long histories)
[02:56] Tom Becker: you mentioned batching — how do you recommend we configure batching vs our latency SLOs? we have bursty traffic and want to keep median < 200ms but minimize cost
[03:10] Diego Alvarez: we generally recommend adaptive batching with a max latency cap. Redwood's runtime supports continuous batching and time-bound batching: you pick a max wait (e.g., 50ms) and a max batch size tuned to GPU. For median <200ms you might set the batch wait to 30-40ms and set concurrency per GPU accordingly. We'll provide a suggested starting config based on your QPS and model size
[03:34] Priya Das: and quantization — our models are 13B and 70B variants, what's the tradeoff for going 4-bit vs 8-bit in private?
[03:44] Marcus Patel: quantization reduces memory and can increase throughput but may slightly degrade quality. For 13B we see minimal perf regression with 4-bit quant, for 70B 4-bit sometimes needs more calibration. On Private deployments you can pick model variants per route so we can route latency-sensitive traffic to a higher precision variant and background jobs to quantized ones
[04:03] Jamal Rivers: that routing sounds useful. Does routing add any network overhead?
[04:09] Sofia Chen: not really network overhead; it's more about model placement. If variants are colocated in the same pool the network path is the same. If you have separate pools in different subnets/AZs then cross-AZ traffic could add 1-3 ms depending on region
[04:22] Tom Becker: on PrivateLink, do we need NAT for outbound access to S3 for model artifacts or can that be done via privatelink to S3 gateway endpoints?
[04:34] Diego Alvarez: you can use gateway endpoints or S3 PrivateLink endpoints to avoid public NAT. For initial model downloads we recommend using presigned URLs via a privatelinked S3 or an internal bastion with controlled egress. That avoids opening NAT for the whole subnet
[04:50] Priya Das: what about health checks and metrics? our ops team wants to scrape metrics internally, will Prometheus scrape endpoints be reachable over the privatelink path?
[05:00] Marcus Patel: yes metrics endpoints can be exposed on the internal interface. We support mTLS and token-based auth on metrics; you'll need to ensure security groups and NACLs allow the monitoring subnets to reach the runtime ENIs
[05:13] Jamal Rivers: are there any gotchas with cross-AZ scaling? we saw inter-AZ bandwidth spikes when autoscaling in another vendor's setup
[05:24] Diego Alvarez: autoscaling can cause temporary cross-AZ model loads and KV warmups. To mitigate we pre-warm model shards and use a rolling scale policy that prefers same-AZ capacity first. Also the runtime's KV prefetch helps amortize cold miss costs
[05:40] Tom Becker: how long does pre-warm take for a 70B model?
[05:44] Marcus Patel: depends on storage and network; with NVMe-backed local cache and high-throughput link, a full load might take minutes; partial warm (autoloading hot layers) can be seconds. We can provide exact numbers in the benchmark spreadsheet.
[05:58] Priya Das: about benchmarks — Jamal wants 95th percentile under 500ms for a 70B gen with context 2k tokens, is that realistic on a 3-node Dedicated pool?
[06:10] Marcus Patel: it's achievable with optimized kernels and batching tuned; 95th for token generation often hits 300-600ms depending on sequence length and QPS. We'll run the 3-node test with your typical prompt shapes and share the spread
[06:23] Jamal Rivers: ok please do. Also curious on encryption: we use customer-managed KMS keys and HSM in some regions, does Redwood Private support CMKs and bring-your-own-hsm?
[06:36] Sofia Chen: yes, our Private control plane supports KMS integration; for on-prem we support HSM integrations for key wrapping. We'll include the security whitepaper, and Diego can follow up with the enterprise security packet
[06:50] Lena Ortiz: can audit logs be exported to our SIEM in real time? we need immutable trails for model access and inference events
[06:58] Diego Alvarez: yes log streaming to your SIEM via Kinesis/CloudWatch/third-party endpoints is supported; we can stream audit logs, API events, and token-level cost traces. We provide configurable retention policies too
[07:12] Priya Das: let's talk about PrivateLink throughput limits; if we have high concurrent small requests does PrivateLink become a bottleneck?
[07:24] Marcus Patel: PrivateLink scales with interface endpoints but there are per-endpoint bandwidth considerations. For high concurrent QPS we recommend a multi-endpoint setup across subnets and AZs, and connection pooling at the client side. The runtime also supports long-lived connections (HTTP/2) to reduce connection churn
[07:42] Tom Becker: connection pooling is fine. For DNS TTLs, if we update endpoints during a failover, how quickly do clients pick up the new IP? we want minimal interruption when routing between Dedicated pools
[07:55] Diego Alvarez: use low DNS TTLs (30s) for ephemeral endpoints and have a multi-endpoint fallback in the client. Also we recommend health-check based routing at the LB layer so clients rarely need to re-resolve on short failovers
[08:10] Jamal Rivers: what's Redwood's recommended network CIDR layout for a dedicated runtime subnet? we want to avoid IP exhaustion if we scale to many GPUs
[08:20] Marcus Patel: we suggest /20 per pool to start; it gives plenty of IPs for pods/ENIs and leaves room for growth. We'll share a template that maps pools to subnets and AZ affinity settings
[08:34] Priya Das: on the topic of KV cache eviction — does the runtime shard cache per model or per request? how do we avoid thundering herd when scaling up?
[08:45] Marcus Patel: cache is sharded per runtime node by keyspace; we use a coordinated backoff and jittered prefetch for warmups to avoid simultaneous heavy loads. On scale-up we do staggered priming and rate-limit initial fetches to prevent thundering herds
[09:00] Tom Becker: minor nit: our security team wants mTLS between our clients and the interface endpoint. Is that supported?
[09:07] Sofia Chen: yes, we support mTLS in front of the runtime as well as token auth. For PrivateLink you'd terminate TLS at the interface endpoint and then mTLS to the runtime if you prefer end-to-end. We'll include config examples
[09:21] Jamal Rivers: any performance difference when using mTLS?
[09:25] Marcus Patel: negligible for steady connections; the main cost is on connection set up. That's why we recommend keep-alive and connection pooling for high QPS
[09:36] Diego Alvarez: quick note on observability — we'll emit per-route latency histograms and token-level traces. Those can be exported to your tracing backend; we can also push alerts on quality regressions tied to prompt sets
[09:50] Priya Das: good. about model artifacts: do you support private registry in our VPC or must models be pulled from Redwood-hosted object store?
[09:59] Sofia Chen: Private deployments can be configured to pull from your S3 with presigned URLs or a private registry; for hosted we host artifacts. For Aurelius we can use your S3 via VPC endpoints to keep artifacts private
[10:12] Jamal Rivers: ok that works. any known gotchas with NAT + egress rules during autoscaling windows?
[10:21] Marcus Patel: yes, if NAT capacity is limited you can get stalled downloads during scale-up; that's why we recommend either PrivateLink to S3 or pre-warmed local artifact cache. If NAT is required ensure you have enough NAT gateways or use managed egress pods behind a scaled pool
[10:36] Tom Becker: final question from networking: if we want full isolation on-prem with air-gapped clusters, what does the Redwood private control plane need?
[10:46] Diego Alvarez: for air-gapped we provide an appliance and an offline onboarding flow; the control plane can be run as a private control plane inside your network and you manage keys. There's a set of topology docs we'll share; it requires an initial bootstrap connection and then can operate disconnected for long periods
[11:00] Priya Das: awesome. anything else on runtime perf we should be aware of?
[11:06] Marcus Patel: one more: token latency variance often comes from heterogenous batch sizes and GPU scheduling; to reduce 95th you'd tune batch caps and use intra-pool placement policies so similar workload types hit the same node types
[11:20] Jamal Rivers: great, let's recap next steps
[11:25] Sofia Chen: recap: Marcus runs the 3-node KV-cache + 70B benchmark and shares numbers; Diego sends PrivateLink + subnet templates and security packet; I send pricing and pilot onboarding steps; customer to share CIDRs and egress constraints. We'll schedule pilot kickoff for week of 2027-09-20.
[11:44] Jamal Rivers: sounds good, thanks everyone
[11:48] Priya Das: thanks
[11:50] Sofia Chen: thanks all, we'll follow up with the artifacts and schedule
[11:55] [call ends]
